pages.title: About the Baker
pages.content:
Hello, I’m Noor

From hotel kitchens to my own little oven

I trained as a pastry chef and spent over a decade working in hotel kitchens, piping hundreds of éclairs before sunrise. I loved the precision, but I missed baking for people I could actually see enjoy it.

Sugar & Saffron began as a notebook of recipes I scaled down for home ovens. Saffron came from my grandmother, who put it in everything from rice to biscuits. Sugar came from me.

Noor

A few facts

  • 12 years in pastry kitchens
  • 200+ tested recipes
  • 3 ovens, one temperamental
  • 1 sourdough starter called Bun

What you will find here

Every recipe is tested at least three times in a regular home oven, with weights in grams and cups where it makes sense. I write down what can go wrong as carefully as what should go right.

Measure carefully, taste often, and never apologise for a second slice.

My kitchen rule

pages.title: Seasonal Collections
pages.content:
Baking with the seasons means better flavour and a reason to look forward to every month. Choose a season to see its recipes.

Spring

Blossoms, rhubarb and the first strawberries.

Summer

Stone fruit, berries and no-fuss bakes.

Autumn

Pears, spice and toasted nuts.

Winter

Citrus, chocolate and festive showstoppers.

How I plan a seasonal bake

  1. Start at the market and see what smells best.
  2. Pick one star ingredient and let it lead.
  3. Add a spice or a flower water to make it feel special.
  4. Keep the rest simple.

posts.title: Saffron & Cardamom Morning Buns
posts.excerpt: Golden, pillowy buns twisted with cardamom sugar and glazed with a whisper of saffron syrup. The bake I make when the first frost arrives.
posts.content:
Every year, on the first morning the windows fog over, I bloom a pinch of saffron in warm milk and the whole kitchen turns gold. These buns are the result: soft, rich and spiralled with cardamom sugar that caramelises at the edges.

The dough is an enriched one, so it is a little sticky at first. Resist the urge to add more flour. A long, slow rise in the fridge overnight does the work for you and makes shaping a dream in the morning.

Jump to the recipe

A few notes before you start

  • Crush the saffron threads with a pinch of sugar for the most colour.
  • Use freshly ground cardamom if you can; the pre-ground kind loses its perfume quickly.
  • The shaped buns can rest in the fridge for up to 16 hours.

Bake them until they are deeply golden. Pale buns are polite buns, and polite is not what we are after.

From my notebook

If you have never twisted buns before, do not worry about perfection. Even the wonky ones come out of the oven looking like they belong in a bakery window.

Saffron & cardamom morning buns

  • Prep40 min
  • Riseovernight
  • Bake18 min
  • Makes12 buns

Ingredients

  • 250 ml whole milk, warmed
  • A generous pinch of saffron threads
  • 7 g instant yeast
  • 500 g strong white flour
  • 60 g caster sugar
  • 1 egg, plus 1 for glazing
  • 80 g soft butter
  • Filling: 100 g butter, 80 g light brown sugar, 2 tsp ground cardamom

Method

  1. Steep the crushed saffron in the warm milk for 15 minutes.
  2. Mix in the yeast, flour, sugar, egg and a pinch of salt, then knead in the butter until glossy.
  3. Cover and chill overnight.
  4. Roll into a rectangle, spread with the filling, fold in thirds and cut into 12 strips.
  5. Twist each strip and knot it into a bun. Prove for 45 minutes until puffy.
  6. Brush with egg and bake at 200°C for 16–18 minutes.

Brush the hot buns with a syrup of 50 g sugar, 50 ml water and a few saffron threads for a glossy finish.

Print this recipe

comments.author: Hanna
comments.content: Made these on Sunday and the house smelled incredible. The overnight rise is genius.

comments.author: Theo
comments.content: Could I use oat milk instead of whole milk?

comments.author: Noor
comments.content: Yes! Oat milk works well; the buns are just a touch less rich.

posts.title: Strawberry & Rose Sponge Cake
posts.excerpt: Two feather-light sponges, rose-scented cream and the first sweet strawberries of the year. A cake for garden tables and long afternoons.
posts.content:
This is the cake I bake for birthdays in May. It is simple at heart, a classic sponge, but a few drops of rose water in the cream make it taste like a garden in bloom.

The secret to a tall, tender sponge is patience: whisk the eggs and sugar until they leave a ribbon trail that sits on the surface for a few seconds before sinking.

Choosing your strawberries

Smaller berries often have more flavour than giant ones. Slice half of them for the middle and keep the prettiest whole for the top, with their green hulls still on.

Assemble the cake no more than an hour before serving so the cream stays light and the sponge does not soften too much.

Leftovers keep in the fridge for a day, covered, though I have rarely had any.

Strawberry & rose sponge

  • Prep30 min
  • Bake22 min
  • Serves10
  • LevelEasy

Ingredients

  • 4 eggs
  • 200 g caster sugar
  • 200 g self-raising flour
  • 200 g butter, melted and cooled
  • 300 ml double cream
  • 1 tsp rose water
  • 2 tbsp icing sugar
  • 400 g strawberries

Method

  1. Heat the oven to 180°C and line two 20 cm tins.
  2. Whisk eggs and sugar until pale and thick, about 6 minutes.
  3. Fold in the flour, then the butter, in three additions.
  4. Divide between the tins and bake for 20–22 minutes.
  5. Whip the cream with rose water and icing sugar to soft peaks.
  6. Layer the cooled sponges with cream and sliced strawberries.

Rose water varies a lot in strength. Add half, taste, then add more.

Print this recipe

comments.author: Mireille
comments.content: The rose cream is so delicate. My mother asked for the recipe straight away!

posts.title: Pistachio Raspberry Financiers
posts.excerpt: Little brown-butter almond cakes with a jewel of raspberry in the middle and a crunch of pistachio on top. Ready in thirty minutes.
posts.content:
Financiers are the little cakes I reach for when friends text to say they are on their way. They are made with egg whites, ground nuts and nutty browned butter, and they come together in one bowl.

Traditionally they are baked in small rectangular moulds, said to resemble gold bars. A mini muffin tin works perfectly well, so do not let the lack of a special mould stop you.

Browning the butter

  1. Melt the butter over a medium heat in a light-coloured pan so you can see it change.
  2. Let it foam, then watch for golden-brown flecks at the bottom.
  3. Pour it into a cold bowl the moment it smells of toasted hazelnuts.

They are best on the day they are baked, while the edges are still crisp. By day two they turn soft and fudgy, which some people prefer.

Pistachio raspberry financiers

  • Prep15 min
  • Bake14 min
  • Makes16
  • LevelEasy

Ingredients

  • 90 g butter
  • 60 g ground almonds
  • 30 g pistachios, finely ground, plus extra to sprinkle
  • 110 g icing sugar
  • 40 g plain flour
  • 3 egg whites
  • 16 raspberries

Method

  1. Brown the butter and let it cool slightly.
  2. Whisk the nuts, sugar and flour, then the egg whites.
  3. Stir in the brown butter until smooth.
  4. Fill buttered moulds two-thirds full and press in a raspberry.
  5. Sprinkle with pistachios and bake at 200°C for 12–14 minutes.
Print this recipe

posts.title: Brown Butter Pecan Blondies
posts.excerpt: Chewy, caramel-edged blondies with toasted pecans and a flake of sea salt. The traybake that disappears first at every bake sale.
posts.content:
A good blondie should taste of butterscotch, with a crackly top and a middle that bends rather than crumbles. Browning the butter and using plenty of dark sugar gets you there.

I toast the pecans until they are fragrant, then chop them roughly so every square has a few big pieces.

Make them your own

  • Swap pecans for walnuts or hazelnuts.
  • Fold in a handful of white chocolate chunks.
  • Ripple through two spoonfuls of salted caramel before baking.

Brown butter pecan blondies

  • Prep20 min
  • Bake28 min
  • Makes16 squares
  • Keeps5 days

Ingredients

  • 170 g butter, browned
  • 220 g dark brown sugar
  • 50 g caster sugar
  • 2 eggs
  • 2 tsp vanilla extract
  • 220 g plain flour
  • 1/2 tsp baking powder
  • 120 g toasted pecans
  • Flaky sea salt

Method

  1. Heat the oven to 175°C and line a 20 cm square tin.
  2. Whisk the warm brown butter with both sugars.
  3. Beat in the eggs and vanilla until glossy.
  4. Fold in flour, baking powder and pecans.
  5. Spread in the tin, sprinkle with salt and bake for 26–28 minutes.
  6. Cool completely before cutting.
Print this recipe

They keep for five days in a tin and freeze beautifully. I cut the whole tray, wrap squares individually and pull one out whenever an afternoon needs rescuing.

comments.author: Ines
comments.content: I added white chocolate and they were gone in an hour. Thank you!

posts.title: Lemon Meringue Tartlets
posts.excerpt: Crisp butter pastry, sharp lemon curd and toasted meringue swirls. Small enough to eat in three bites, pretty enough for a celebration.
posts.content:
A lemon tart should make you pucker just a little. I make the curd with plenty of zest and only enough sugar to round it off, then pile soft meringue on top for contrast.

You can make every part of these ahead: the pastry cases keep in a tin for three days and the curd keeps in the fridge for a week. Top with meringue just before serving.

The pastry

I use a simple sweet shortcrust with icing sugar, which gives a fine, sandy texture. Keep everything cold and handle it as little as you can.

Lemon meringue tartlets

  • Prep1 hr
  • Chill30 min
  • Bake25 min
  • Makes12

Ingredients

  • Pastry: 200 g plain flour, 120 g cold butter, 50 g icing sugar, 1 egg yolk
  • Curd: zest and juice of 3 lemons, 120 g sugar, 3 eggs, 90 g butter
  • Meringue: 3 egg whites, 150 g caster sugar

Method

  1. Rub the butter into flour and sugar, bind with the yolk and chill.
  2. Line 12 tartlet tins, chill again, then blind bake at 180°C for 15 minutes.
  3. Cook the curd ingredients gently, stirring, until thick. Strain and cool.
  4. Fill the cases with curd.
  5. Whisk the whites to stiff peaks, adding sugar a spoonful at a time.
  6. Pipe swirls on top and toast with a torch or under a hot grill.
Print this recipe

comments.author: Clara
comments.content: Beautiful! Do the cases go soft once filled?

comments.author: Noor
comments.content: They stay crisp for about six hours. Brushing the baked cases with a little egg white helps.

posts.title: Spiced Pear Frangipane Tart
posts.excerpt: Poached pears fanned over almond cream in a crisp tart shell, with cinnamon, clove and a glaze of apricot jam.
posts.content:
When pears arrive at the market, this tart appears on my table every Sunday until they are gone. Poaching them in spiced syrup first means they stay juicy and hold their shape.

Frangipane is an almond cream that puffs gently around the fruit as it bakes. It is forgiving, quick to make and tastes wonderful warm or cold.

Fanning the pears

Halve and core the poached pears, then slice each half thinly across, keeping the slices together. Slide a palette knife underneath, press gently to fan them, and lift them onto the frangipane.

Use pears that are ripe but still firm. Conference and Bosc are my favourites.

A spoonful of crème fraîche on the side is all it needs.

Spiced pear frangipane tart

  • Prep45 min
  • Bake40 min
  • Serves8
  • LevelIntermediate

Ingredients

  • 1 sweet pastry case, blind baked (23 cm)
  • 4 pears, peeled
  • 500 ml water, 150 g sugar, 1 cinnamon stick, 3 cloves
  • 125 g butter, soft
  • 125 g caster sugar
  • 2 eggs
  • 125 g ground almonds
  • 2 tbsp apricot jam

Method

  1. Poach the pears in the spiced syrup for 15 minutes; cool.
  2. Beat butter and sugar, then the eggs, then fold in the almonds.
  3. Spread the frangipane in the tart case.
  4. Fan the sliced pear halves over the top.
  5. Bake at 180°C for 35–40 minutes until golden.
  6. Warm the jam with a spoon of syrup and brush over the tart.
Print this recipe

posts.title: Chocolate Orange Yule Log
posts.excerpt: A rolled chocolate sponge filled with orange-scented cream and covered in glossy ganache bark. Festive, and easier than it looks.
posts.content:
Every winter I promise myself a simpler dessert, and every winter I make this yule log anyway. It looks grand, but it is really a thin sponge rolled around whipped cream.

The trick to a roll that does not crack is to roll the sponge while it is still warm, in a clean tea towel dusted with cocoa, then let it cool in that shape.

Decorating

  • Drag a fork through the ganache to make bark lines.
  • Dust with icing sugar for snow.
  • Add candied orange slices and a sprig of rosemary.

Cracks are fine. Ganache covers a multitude of sins.

Said every December

Chocolate orange yule log

  • Prep50 min
  • Bake12 min
  • Serves10
  • LevelIntermediate

Ingredients

  • 4 eggs
  • 100 g caster sugar
  • 65 g plain flour
  • 25 g cocoa
  • 300 ml double cream
  • Zest of 1 orange
  • 200 g dark chocolate
  • 200 ml cream for the ganache

Method

  1. Whisk eggs and sugar until tripled in volume.
  2. Sift in flour and cocoa and fold gently.
  3. Spread in a lined Swiss roll tin and bake at 200°C for 10–12 minutes.
  4. Roll up in a cocoa-dusted towel and cool.
  5. Whip the cream with zest, unroll, fill and re-roll.
  6. Cover with ganache and decorate.
Print this recipe

comments.author: Pieter
comments.content: Made this for New Year's Eve. It looked like it came from a patisserie.

posts.title: How I Keep Pastry Cold (and Why It Matters)
posts.excerpt: Flaky, tender pastry comes down to temperature. Here are the small habits from my years in pastry kitchens that make the biggest difference.
posts.content:
The first thing I learned in a professional kitchen was that pastry is all about temperature. Butter that stays cold makes steam in the oven, and steam makes layers.

You do not need a marble counter or a walk-in fridge. You just need a few habits, and a willingness to put things back in the fridge more often than feels necessary.

My cold-pastry habits

  1. Cube the butter and freeze it for ten minutes before you start.
  2. Use ice water, measured from a jug with ice still floating in it.
  3. Mix with your fingertips, never your palms.
  4. Chill the dough after mixing, after rolling and after lining the tin.
  5. If the butter looks shiny or greasy, stop and chill everything for fifteen minutes.

When it goes wrong

Shrinking pastry has usually been stretched or not rested. Soggy bases often need a hotter oven or a baking tray preheated underneath the tin. Tough pastry was probably worked too much; next time, stop mixing as soon as it holds together.

Cold hands, warm heart, and an extra shelf in the fridge.

Pastry kitchen proverb, more or less

comments.author: Sami
comments.content: Freezing the butter cubes changed everything for me. Thank you for this.
